# Wyrd — full machine-readable reference

> Wyrd is open-source AI assurance and verification infrastructure. Verify AI systems before and after release, with verdicts you can trace, reproduce, and audit.

Every published docs page in sidebar order, generated from the docs content tree. Links are relative to the docs base /wyrd/ (published at https://docs.bohmian.ai/wyrd/). The page index is [llms.txt](/wyrd/llms.txt).

## Start here

Set up a local server, then run one verification, in this order. A connected Wyrd MCP server teaches the same route through `wyrd.guide {"topic":"start"}`.

- [Set up Wyrd](/wyrd/get-started/setup/): install Wyrd and start a local server you keep running.
- [Run your first verification](/wyrd/get-started/quickstart/): declare a Verifier in YAML and verify a passing and a failing support answer from Python, Rust, or TypeScript.

# What Wyrd does

Page: /wyrd/get-started/introduction/

> Wyrd verifies what your AI system does against the requirements you declare, and records which versions produced each result.

You ship a support agent, a Q&A bot, or a model behind an API. Wyrd checks what it says against the rules you set, such as "never promise a refund" or "answer from the policy document", before you release a change and while it serves real traffic. When a rule fails, Wyrd tells you which rule, why, and which version of your system broke it.

## How Wyrd fits your stack

_Diagram `wyrd-in-your-stack`: see the web page._

1. **Declare.** Describe what you ship in YAML (a Service and its Agents, Models, and Data) and bind Verifiers to any of them. Declare them from CI with `wyrd declare` or from your code. Each declaration has a version, so a changed prompt is a new version.
2. **Observe.** Your app sends Bifrost, Wyrd's data plane, everything it produces as it runs: telemetry, its own data, and the evidence it submits to verify. Bifrost keeps all of it queryable with SQL beside every verdict.
3. **Verify.** Your app sends a result to a Verifier and gets a verdict for each requirement, with a reason. Wyrd keeps every verdict with the exact versions it judged.

Your coding agent reads the same declarations, verdicts, and evidence over MCP. The Python, Rust, and TypeScript SDKs, the CLI, MCP, and HTTP all call one server, so a verdict reads the same from each. [Architecture](/wyrd/understand/architecture/) shows what a team deployment runs.

## An example

A support agent must never promise a guaranteed refund. The Service describes the agent and binds a Verifier, which states that requirement as an assertion:

**support-reply.yaml**

```yaml title="support-reply.yaml"
# The subject: your support agent's Service, verified by no-refund-promise.
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: support-reply
  version: 1.0.0
spec:
  verified_by:
    - verifier: ./no-refund-promise.yaml

```

**no-refund-promise.yaml**

```yaml title="no-refund-promise.yaml"
# The Verifier: a support answer never promises a guaranteed refund.
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Verifier
metadata:
  name: no-refund-promise
  version: 1.0.0
spec:
  inputs:
    answer: { type: json }
  requirements:
    - id: no-refund-promise
      statement: The answer never promises a guaranteed refund
      check:
        kind: assert
        path: inputs.answer
        operator: not_contains
        expected: guaranteed refund

```

This program declares both and verifies two answers:

**Python**

```python title="quickstart.py"
from wyrd import WyrdState

# Declare the Service and the Verifier it references, and get a ready state.
state = WyrdState.declare("support-reply.yaml")
run = state.run()

for answer in ("Your refund request is approved.", "You have a guaranteed refund."):
    result = run.observe.verify("no-refund-promise", answer=answer)
    print(f"{result.verdict}: {result.requirements[0]['reason']}")
    print(f"  subject:  {result.subject}")
    print(f"  verifier: {result.verifier}")

```

**Rust**

```rust title="src/main.rs"
//! The docsite Quickstart in Rust: declare a Service and the Verifier it
//! references, then judge a passing and a failing answer.

use wyrd_ai::WyrdError;
use wyrd_ai::serde_json::json;
use wyrd_ai::state::WyrdState;

/// Declares `support-reply.yaml` from the working directory, verifies two
/// answers against `no-refund-promise`, and prints each verdict with its reason
/// and the exact subject and Verifier identities.
///
/// # Errors
///
/// Returns the [`WyrdError`] of a refused declaration or verification.
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), WyrdError> {
    // Declare the Service and the Verifier it references, and get a ready state.
    let state = WyrdState::declare("support-reply.yaml").await?;
    let run = state.run();

    for answer in [
        "Your refund request is approved.",
        "You have a guaranteed refund.",
    ] {
        let result = run
            .observe()
            .verify("no-refund-promise", json!(answer))
            .await?;
        let reason = &result.outcome.requirements[0].reason;
        println!("{}: {reason}", result.outcome.verdict);
        println!("  subject:  {}", result.subject);
        println!("  verifier: {}", result.verifier);
    }
    Ok(())
}

```

**TypeScript**

```typescript title="quickstart.ts"
import { type CardRef, WyrdState } from "wyrd-ai";

// Declare the Service and the Verifier it references, and get a ready state.
const state = await WyrdState.declare("support-reply.yaml");
const run = state.run();

const id = (ref: CardRef) => `${ref.kind}/${ref.name}@${ref.version}#${ref.uid}`;
for (const answer of ["Your refund request is approved.", "You have a guaranteed refund."]) {
  const result = await run.observe.verify("no-refund-promise", { answer });
  console.log(`${result.outcome.verdict}: ${result.outcome.requirements[0].reason}`);
  console.log(`  subject:  ${id(result.subject)}`);
  console.log(`  verifier: ${id(result.verifier)}`);
}

```

```text
passed: the comparison held
  subject:  default/Service/support-reply@1.0.0#<uid>
  verifier: default/Verifier/no-refund-promise@1.0.0#<uid>
failed: operator NotContains returned false
  subject:  default/Service/support-reply@1.0.0#<uid>
  verifier: default/Verifier/no-refund-promise@1.0.0#<uid>
```

In CI, `wyrd declare support-reply.yaml` declares the same files from the command line. A check can also ask a model to judge, such as whether a letter follows your refund policy.

## Where Wyrd stops

Wyrd verifies your system; your code runs it. Your app owns its code, models, and data, runs and deploys them, and decides what to do with a verdict. Wyrd is not an application runtime, model host, training framework, or general-purpose code executor.

## Next

[Set up Wyrd](/wyrd/get-started/setup/) starts a local server. [Run your first verification](/wyrd/get-started/quickstart/) then declares a Verifier and verifies one passing and one failing reply.

# Set up Wyrd

Page: /wyrd/get-started/setup/

> Install the Wyrd 0.3.0 CLI and SDK for Python, Rust, or TypeScript, then let your coding agent start a local server and run a first verification, or do it by hand.

Install Wyrd, then set up the rest with your coding agent or by hand. Either way you end with a local server running and your code connected to it.

## What you need

| | Minimum |
| --- | --- |
| OS | macOS on Apple silicon, or Linux (x86_64 or arm64) |
| PostgreSQL | 16, with a user that owns the database (not a superuser) |
| Language | Python 3.11, Rust 1.95, or Node.js 22.18 |

## Install

**Python**

```bash
uv init quickstart && cd quickstart
uv add "wyrd-ai==0.3.0"
```

Run the CLI as `uv run wyrd`.

**Rust**

```bash
cargo install wyrd-cli --version 0.3.0 --locked
cargo new quickstart && cd quickstart
cargo add wyrd-ai@0.3.0 tokio --features tokio/full
```

**TypeScript**

```bash
mkdir quickstart && cd quickstart
pnpm init && pnpm pkg set type=module
pnpm add wyrd-ai@0.3.0
```

Run the CLI as `pnpm wyrd`.

## Agent-guided setup

Let your coding agent finish the setup. Wyrd starts a local server and connects your agent to it, and the agent writes and runs your first verification. Without a coding agent, use [Manual setup](#manual-setup).

In `quickstart`, run:

```bash
wyrd init guided
```

It asks for:

- the coding agent to use
- your database URL, `postgresql://USER:PASSWORD@HOST:5432/DATABASE`
- a tenant name, such as `acme`

If a model provider key such as `OPENAI_API_KEY` is set, it also offers to add that provider to the gateway. Press Enter to skip; the quickstart calls no model.

It then starts a local server and hands over to the agent, which runs [Run your first verification](/wyrd/get-started/quickstart/) and reports one `passed` and one `failed` verdict. Leave the terminal open; the server runs until you press Ctrl-C.

**Another agent, or your own:**

Name the agent with `--host`, such as `wyrd init guided --host claude-code`. For an agent `wyrd` does not launch, start the server by hand, then paste the output of `wyrd init --print-prompt`, or select the Wyrd MCP prompt `setup`.

## Manual setup

### 1. Start the server

In its own terminal, in `quickstart`:

```bash
wyrd init
```

Enter your database URL and a tenant name when asked, and decline the other offers. When it prints this, it's ready:

```text
Local Wyrd ready at http://127.0.0.1:8080 for tenant acme.
```

It also prints a root credential once. Save it; it recovers a lost tenant key.

**Start it without prompts:**

```bash
export WYRD_DATABASE_URL=postgresql://USER:PASSWORD@HOST:5432/DATABASE
wyrd init --tenant acme --non-interactive
```

If an input is missing, it names every missing input and exits before changing anything. Add `--format json` to print one line of JSON when ready.

`wyrd init --help` lists every option.

### 2. Check it works

In a second terminal, in `quickstart`:

```bash
wyrd list
```

An empty list means you're connected. Your code finds the server the same way, with no configuration.

### 3. Run your first verification

Follow [Run your first verification](/wyrd/get-started/quickstart/), through [Confirm the stored verdicts](/wyrd/get-started/quickstart/#3-confirm-the-stored-verdicts).

## If it fails

| You see | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `is a superuser` or `BYPASSRLS` | Use a database user that isn't a superuser |
| `WYRD_CLI_503_SERVER_DEV` naming `listener` | Port 8080 is taken: rerun with `--bind 127.0.0.1:18080` |
| `WYRD_CLIENT_401_NO_CREDENTIALS` | Unset `WYRD_CONFIG_HOME`, `WYRD_API_KEY`, and `WYRD_SERVER_URL`, or match the server terminal |
| `WYRD_CLI_503_SERVER_DEV` naming `guided setup` | Install the agent so its command is on `PATH`, or name an installed one with `--host` |

## Next

[Run your first verification](/wyrd/get-started/quickstart/).

# Run your first verification

Page: /wyrd/get-started/quickstart/

> Declare a Verifier and the Service it checks in two YAML files, then verify a passing and a failing support answer from one Python, Rust, or TypeScript program.

You write two small YAML files and one short program in Python, Rust, or TypeScript. The program declares them to your server, then asks Wyrd to verify two support answers against one requirement: the answer never promises a guaranteed refund. One answer passes and one fails, and each verdict names the exact versions that produced it.

No model, provider key, or application is involved: you supply each answer as text.

## Prerequisites

- The server from [Set up Wyrd](/wyrd/get-started/setup/), running in its own terminal.
- The `quickstart` directory from setup, with the SDK for your language installed. Run everything below there, in a second terminal.

## 1. Declare the requirement

Save the Verifier in your `quickstart` directory as `no-refund-promise.yaml`. Its one requirement checks that the input named `answer` never contains `guaranteed refund`:

```yaml title="no-refund-promise.yaml"
# The Verifier: a support answer never promises a guaranteed refund.
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Verifier
metadata:
  name: no-refund-promise
  version: 1.0.0
spec:
  inputs:
    answer: { type: json }
  requirements:
    - id: no-refund-promise
      statement: The answer never promises a guaranteed refund
      check:
        kind: assert
        path: inputs.answer
        operator: not_contains
        expected: guaranteed refund

```

Save the subject beside it as `support-reply.yaml`. It is a Service, and `verified_by` binds the Verifier to it by relative path:

```yaml title="support-reply.yaml"
# The subject: your support agent's Service, verified by no-refund-promise.
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: support-reply
  version: 1.0.0
spec:
  verified_by:
    - verifier: ./no-refund-promise.yaml

```

## 2. Verify two answers

Save the program and run it from the `quickstart` directory, so it finds both YAML files there:

**Python**

```python title="quickstart.py"
from wyrd import WyrdState

# Declare the Service and the Verifier it references, and get a ready state.
state = WyrdState.declare("support-reply.yaml")
run = state.run()

for answer in ("Your refund request is approved.", "You have a guaranteed refund."):
    result = run.observe.verify("no-refund-promise", answer=answer)
    print(f"{result.verdict}: {result.requirements[0]['reason']}")
    print(f"  subject:  {result.subject}")
    print(f"  verifier: {result.verifier}")

```

```bash
uv run quickstart.py
```

**Rust**

```rust title="src/main.rs"
//! The docsite Quickstart in Rust: declare a Service and the Verifier it
//! references, then judge a passing and a failing answer.

use wyrd_ai::WyrdError;
use wyrd_ai::serde_json::json;
use wyrd_ai::state::WyrdState;

/// Declares `support-reply.yaml` from the working directory, verifies two
/// answers against `no-refund-promise`, and prints each verdict with its reason
/// and the exact subject and Verifier identities.
///
/// # Errors
///
/// Returns the [`WyrdError`] of a refused declaration or verification.
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), WyrdError> {
    // Declare the Service and the Verifier it references, and get a ready state.
    let state = WyrdState::declare("support-reply.yaml").await?;
    let run = state.run();

    for answer in [
        "Your refund request is approved.",
        "You have a guaranteed refund.",
    ] {
        let result = run
            .observe()
            .verify("no-refund-promise", json!(answer))
            .await?;
        let reason = &result.outcome.requirements[0].reason;
        println!("{}: {reason}", result.outcome.verdict);
        println!("  subject:  {}", result.subject);
        println!("  verifier: {}", result.verifier);
    }
    Ok(())
}

```

```bash
cargo run
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript title="quickstart.ts"
import { type CardRef, WyrdState } from "wyrd-ai";

// Declare the Service and the Verifier it references, and get a ready state.
const state = await WyrdState.declare("support-reply.yaml");
const run = state.run();

const id = (ref: CardRef) => `${ref.kind}/${ref.name}@${ref.version}#${ref.uid}`;
for (const answer of ["Your refund request is approved.", "You have a guaranteed refund."]) {
  const result = await run.observe.verify("no-refund-promise", { answer });
  console.log(`${result.outcome.verdict}: ${result.outcome.requirements[0].reason}`);
  console.log(`  subject:  ${id(result.subject)}`);
  console.log(`  verifier: ${id(result.verifier)}`);
}

```

```bash
node quickstart.ts
```

`verify` sends each answer as the Verifier's `answer` input and returns its verdict. Every language prints the same:

```text
passed: the comparison held
  subject:  default/Service/support-reply@1.0.0#<uid>
  verifier: default/Verifier/no-refund-promise@1.0.0#<uid>
failed: operator NotContains returned false
  subject:  default/Service/support-reply@1.0.0#<uid>
  verifier: default/Verifier/no-refund-promise@1.0.0#<uid>
```

Each verdict names the exact version of the Service and Verifier it checked. Your `uid` values differ; the server assigns them.

The second verdict is `failed`, and it is still a successful call: the check ran, and the answer promises a guaranteed refund.

Run the program again. Nothing changed, so you get the same verdicts and `uid` values.

## 3. Confirm the stored verdicts

The server keeps every verdict as evidence, grouped by the Run that produced it. Run `wyrd` as in setup (`uv run wyrd` in Python, `pnpm wyrd` in TypeScript). Read the Service to get its `uid`, the one the verdicts printed after `#`:

```bash
wyrd get --kind Service --name support-reply --version 1.0.0
```

Its `metadata.uid` is the Service's `uid`. Save this query as `stored-verdicts.sql`, with `<uid>` replaced by that value:

```sql title="stored-verdicts.sql"
-- Replace <uid> with the Service's metadata.uid from wyrd get.
SELECT result_id, run_id, card_uid, verdict FROM vala.verification.results WHERE card_uid = '<uid>' ORDER BY ended_at DESC LIMIT 20

```

Run it against the address `wyrd init` printed:

```bash
wyrd query --server http://127.0.0.1:8080 --file stored-verdicts.sql
```

It prints one JSON row per stored verdict, newest first:

```text
{"result_id":"<id>","run_id":"<run_id>","card_uid":"<uid>","verdict":"failed"}
{"result_id":"<id>","run_id":"<run_id>","card_uid":"<uid>","verdict":"passed"}
```

The `failed` and `passed` rows with the same `run_id` are your program's two verdicts, and that `run_id` identifies its Run. The server publishes rows shortly after the program ends: if a verdict is missing, repeat the query for up to a minute.

## 4. Change the requirement

Edit `no-refund-promise.yaml` to `expected: guaranteed` and run the program again. It stops with `WYRD_REGISTRY_409_SPEC_DRIFT`: `no-refund-promise@1.0.0` already means the declaration that checks `guaranteed refund`, and a version never changes meaning.

To change the requirement, give it a new version: set `version: 1.1.0` in `no-refund-promise.yaml`. The Service now references different content too, so set its `version: 1.1.0` as well. Run again, and the verdicts name `support-reply@1.1.0` and `no-refund-promise@1.1.0`.

## If it fails

| You see | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `transport unavailable` | Start the server as in [Set up Wyrd](/wyrd/get-started/setup/#1-start-the-server) |
| `WYRD_CLIENT_401_NO_CREDENTIALS` | Use the same `WYRD_CONFIG_HOME` as the server terminal |
| `WYRD_LOADER_400_INVALID_ENVELOPE` | Run from the directory that holds both YAML files |
| No rows after a minute | Check that `<uid>` is the `metadata.uid` that `wyrd get` printed |

## Next

[How verification works](/wyrd/understand/how-verification-works/) explains requirements, checks, and verdicts. The [Verifier reference](/wyrd/reference/verifier-card/) lists every field you can declare.

# Use with your coding agent

Page: /wyrd/get-started/use-with-your-coding-agent/

> Give your coding agent the Wyrd docs through llms.txt and Wyrd's tools through MCP with wyrd mcp install.

Point your coding agent at the Wyrd docs, then connect it to your Wyrd server so it can read your declarations, verdicts, and evidence.

## Give your agent the docs

| File | URL | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`llms.txt`](/wyrd/llms.txt) | `https://docs.bohmian.ai/wyrd/llms.txt` | An index of every page, with where to start |
| [`llms-full.txt`](/wyrd/llms-full.txt) | `https://docs.bohmian.ai/wyrd/llms-full.txt` | Every page in full, with its YAML and code |

Paste either URL into your agent's chat, or add it to the agent's project instructions.

## Connect your agent over MCP

Starting from scratch? [`wyrd init guided`](/wyrd/get-started/setup/#agent-guided-setup) starts the server, connects your agent, and has it set up your project. To connect an agent to a server that is already running, you need the agent installed and opened once.

```bash
wyrd mcp install --host claude-code
```

```text
claude-code: added /Users/you/.claude.json
```

Run `wyrd mcp install` without `--host` to pick from the agents it finds. Restart the agent to load the entry. The agent starts `wyrd mcp proxy`, which signs each call with the credential `wyrd init` saved; the agent's configuration file never holds it.

| Agent | `--host` |
| --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `claude-code` |
| Codex CLI and IDE | `codex` |
| Cursor | `cursor` |
| GitHub Copilot CLI | `copilot-cli` |
| GitHub Copilot in VS Code | `vscode` |
| Pi | `pi` |
| Hermes Agent | `hermes` |

## Check it worked

Ask your agent:

```text
Call the wyrd.guide tool with topic "start" and summarize what it says.
```

The agent calls `wyrd.guide` and describes the Declare → Observe → Verify workflow. Read tools work at once; write tools need a credential with the matching role. [MCP tools](/wyrd/reference/mcp-tools/) lists every tool and its permission.

## Advanced

### Connect to a deployed server

Sign in to the server, then name it when you install:

```bash
wyrd auth login --server https://wyrd.example.com --tenant acme
wyrd mcp install --host claude-code --server https://wyrd.example.com
```

The URL is stored in that agent's entry only. Remote servers must use `https://`.

## If it fails

| You see | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `WYRD_CLI_400_MCP_HOST_SELECTION`, `detected: none` | Install and open the agent once, then rerun |
| `<host>: conflict: … has a wyrd entry that does not run wyrd mcp proxy` | Rename or remove the other `wyrd` entry, then rerun |
| The agent log has `WYRD_CLI_401_NO_CREDENTIALS` | Run `wyrd init`, or `wyrd auth login` for a deployed server |
| The agent log has `WYRD_CLIENT_503_TRANSPORT_DOWN` | Start the server, then restart the agent |

## Next

[Run your first verification](/wyrd/get-started/quickstart/), then ask your agent to explain its verdicts.

# Services

Page: /wyrd/build-and-verify/declare/define-a-service/

> Declare a Service from YAML files, with each component at an exact version and a table for the rows it records, then read back what the server stored.

Declare the Service your app runs: the components it is built from, each at an exact version, and the tables it records rows into. Every verdict then names exactly what it checked.

You need a running server from [Set up Wyrd](/wyrd/get-started/setup/). This page builds the `support-desk` Service; the finished files are in `examples/support-desk-app/service/`.

## 1. Write the components

Each component is its own YAML file with an exact `metadata.version`. The support desk has an Agent and the Prompt it runs, and the Agent points at the Prompt by relative path:

**support-agent.yaml**

```yaml title="support-agent.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Agent
metadata:
  name: support-agent
  version: 1.0.0
spec:
  prompt: ./support-prompt.yaml
  execution_route:
    kind: wyrd_gateway
    deployment: openai
  tool_names: []
  run_config:
    max_iterations: 1

```

**support-prompt.yaml**

```yaml title="support-prompt.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Prompt
metadata:
  name: support-prompt
  version: 1.0.0
spec:
  provider: openai
  model: gpt-4o
  messages:
  - role: user
    content: 'Answer the customer: {{question}}'

```

`execution_route` says how the Agent reaches its model: `wyrd_gateway` sends it through the [LLM gateway](/wyrd/connect/set-up-the-llm-gateway/) deployment named `openai`. Use `{kind: native}` when your own code calls the model.

A hosted model such as `gpt-4o` needs no file of its own. Declare a `Model` only for a model you own and version, such as a trained classifier, so verdicts attach to its exact version.

## 2. Write the Service

The Service gives each component an `alias`, the name your code uses at runtime, such as `run.for_card("agent")`:

```yaml title="support-desk.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: support-desk
  version: 1.0.0
  space: default
spec:
  service_type: agent
  tables:
    - name: tickets  # becomes vala.datasets.tickets
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:  # in column order
          question: {type: string}
          answer: {type: string}
        required: [question, answer]
  components:
    - alias: agent
      ref: ./support-agent.yaml  # relative to this file
    - alias: prompt
      ref: ./support-prompt.yaml
```

A `ref` can also name a component that is already declared, such as `{kind: Model, name: churn-classifier, version: 1.4.2}`. Every reference names one exact version, never a range.

## 3. Check it

```bash
wyrd declare --check support-desk.yaml
```

It loads the Service and every file it references, validates them without contacting the server, and lists each one. Fix anything it reports before you declare.

## 4. Declare it

```bash
wyrd declare support-desk.yaml
```

It declares every file the Service references, dependencies first, creates the `tickets` table, and prints one line per file with its outcome. Run it again: unchanged files come back `idempotent_noop`, so declaring is safe to repeat.

**From code:**

`WyrdState.declare("support-desk.yaml")` declares the same files and returns the Service ready to use, as in [Write a Verifier](/wyrd/build-and-verify/verify/author-a-verifier/#3-call-it-and-read-the-verdict).

## 5. Read it back

The server records which component references which, in both directions. Fetch the Service and list its components:

**Python**

```python
from wyrd.cards import CardRef, Cards

card = Cards().get(CardRef("Service", "support-desk", "1.0.0", space="default"))
for edge in card.relationships["outbound_refs"]:
    print(edge.get("alias"), edge["ref"])
```

**Rust**

```rust
use wyrd_ai::cards::{CardRef, CardSelector, Cards};

let service: CardRef = "default/Service/support-desk@1.0.0".parse()?;
let card = Cards::connect().await?.get(CardSelector::exact(service)).await?;
for edge in &card.relationships.outbound_refs {
    println!("{edge:?}");
}
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
import { Cards } from "wyrd-ai";

const card = await (await Cards.connect()).get("default/Service/support-desk@1.0.0");
for (const edge of card.relationships.outbound_refs) console.log(edge.alias, edge.ref);
```

It prints one line per component, with its alias and exact version. Fetching `support-prompt` instead shows, under `inbound_refs`, both the Agent and the Service that use it.

## 6. Change a component

A declared version never changes. To change the Prompt, set a new `version` in `support-prompt.yaml`, then bump the Agent and the Service that reference it, since they now point at different content. Declare again: the new Service version records the new Prompt, and verdicts from the old version still name the old one.

**Set the space once:**

`space` groups related files, such as a team's. Instead of writing it in every file, put a `wyrd.toml` next to them or in a parent directory:

```toml
[defaults]
space = "support"
```

A file's own `metadata.space` still wins.

## If it fails

| You see | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `WYRD_LOADER_400_INVALID_ENVELOPE` | Fix the file `details.diagnostics` names: a missing `apiVersion` or `kind`, a path to no file, or a missing exact `version` |
| `WYRD_REGISTRY_409_SPEC_DRIFT` | That version is already declared with different content: bump its `version` |
| `WYRD_REGISTRY_422_UNRESOLVED_DEPENDENCY` | Declare the referenced component first, or fix the `ref` |
| `WYRD_VALA_409_BIFROST_FINGERPRINT_MISMATCH` | The table exists with different columns: keep its schema, or use a new table name |

## Next

[Bind a Verifier](/wyrd/build-and-verify/declare/bind-a-verifier/) to say how the Service is checked.

# Bindings

Page: /wyrd/build-and-verify/declare/bind-a-verifier/

> Attach a Verifier to a Service or one of its components with verified_by, and choose whether your code or a schedule runs it.

Attach each Verifier to what it checks, and choose who runs it: your code, or a schedule.

This page uses the `support-desk` Service from [Services](/wyrd/build-and-verify/declare/define-a-service/). The Verifiers it binds are written in [Write a Verifier](/wyrd/build-and-verify/verify/author-a-verifier/).

## 1. Bind Verifiers your code calls

Add a `verified_by` list to the Service, or to one of its components. Each entry names a Verifier file:

```yaml title="support-desk.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: support-desk
  version: 1.0.0
spec:
  service_type: agent
  # The Service's own Verifier checks every answer the desk gives.
  verified_by:
    - verifier: ./no-refund-promise.yaml
  tables:
    - name: tickets
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          question: {type: string}
          answer: {type: string}
        required: [question, answer]
  components:
    - alias: agent
      ref: ./support-agent.yaml
      verified_by:
        - verifier: ./ticket-complete.yaml
        - verifier: ./follows-policy.yaml
    - alias: prompt
      ref: ./support-prompt.yaml

```

Where you bind a Verifier decides where your code calls it:

| Bound on | Call it as |
| --- | --- |
| The Service | `run.observe.verify("no-refund-promise", ...)` |
| The `agent` component | `run.for_card("agent").observe.verify("ticket-complete", ...)` |

Check the bindings:

```bash
wyrd declare --check support-desk.yaml
```

It lists the Service, its components, and each bound Verifier. A Verifier with no `runs_on` runs only when your code calls `verify` or `submit`, as in [Runs and observations](/wyrd/build-and-verify/observe/record-a-run-and-observations/).

## 2. Run a Verifier on a schedule

A schedule judges samples your service recorded over time, such as request latency, instead of one request. Add `runs_on` with a Trigger:

```yaml title="latency-watch.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: latency-watch
  version: 1.0.0
  space: default
spec:
  verified_by:
    - verifier: ./latency-shift.yaml
      runs_on: {kind: schedule, cron: "0 0 * * *"}  # midnight; add tz to use another zone than UTC
```

Only a Verifier whose inputs are `samples` can run on a schedule. The [drift recipe](/wyrd/build-and-verify/verify/verifier-recipes/#drift) writes one.

## 3. React to a failure

Add `on_failure` with the Operators to run after a `failed` verdict:

**latency-watch.yaml**

```yaml title="latency-watch.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: latency-watch
  version: 1.0.0
spec:
  verified_by:
    - verifier: ./latency-shift.yaml
      runs_on: ./daily.yaml
      on_failure:
        - ./alert-on-call.yaml

```

**daily.yaml**

```yaml title="daily.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Trigger
metadata:
  name: daily
  version: 1.0.0
spec:
  description: Once a day at midnight UTC.
  kind: schedule
  cron: "0 0 * * *"

```

**alert-on-call.yaml**

```yaml title="alert-on-call.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Operator
metadata:
  name: alert-on-call
  version: 1.0.0
spec:
  description: Page the on-call hook when latency shifts. The origin comes from the connection.
  kind: http
  method: post
  url: /hooks/latency-shift
  auth:
    scheme: bearer
    connection: on-call-hooks
  body:
    execution_id: "{{execution_id}}"
    summary: "{{summary}}"

```

The Trigger now lives in its own file, so several bindings can share it. Each day at midnight UTC, the server judges the day's `latency` samples and, on a `failed` verdict, posts to the on-call hook. Declaring an `on_failure` binding needs the `operators:invoke` permission.

**Judge a whole conversation:**

A `group_end` Trigger judges every turn sharing a `group_id` once the conversation goes quiet, and `on_verdict_change` runs Operators when that verdict changes. See the [grouped recipe](/wyrd/build-and-verify/verify/verifier-recipes/#grouped-session).

## Binding fields

| Field | Required | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `verifier` | Yes | A path to the Verifier's file, or a declared Verifier |
| `runs_on` | No | A `schedule` or `group_end` Trigger, as a path, a declared Trigger, or inline. Absent, only your code runs the Verifier |
| `on_failure` | No | Operators to run after a `failed` verdict. Not allowed with `group_end` |
| `on_verdict_change` | No | Operators to run when a `group_end` verdict changes |

Any other field is rejected.

## If it fails

| You see | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `WYRD_SDK_404_UNKNOWN_VERIFIER` from `verify` or `submit` | Call it on the Service or component that binds it, or add the binding |
| `WYRD_SPEC_400_DUPLICATE_VERIFICATION_BINDING` | The same Verifier is bound twice on one subject: remove one |
| `WYRD_SPEC_400_TRIGGER_ACTIVATION_MISMATCH` | A schedule is set on a Verifier that doesn't judge `samples`: remove `runs_on` and call it from code |
| `WYRD_PERMISSION_403_DENIED_RBAC` when you declare | Declare `on_failure` with a credential that has `operators:invoke` |

## Next

[Declare the Service](/wyrd/build-and-verify/declare/define-a-service/#4-declare-it), then [verify inside a Run](/wyrd/build-and-verify/observe/record-a-run-and-observations/).

# Runs and observations

Page: /wyrd/build-and-verify/observe/record-a-run-and-observations/

> Wrap each request in a Run, call your model through the gateway, record what happened, verify it, and read the whole Run back.

Wrap each request your app handles in a Run. Everything inside it (the model call, the rows you record, and each verdict) is tied to that Run and to the exact Card version that produced it, so you can read the whole request back with one query.

You need the support-desk Service from [Write a Verifier](/wyrd/build-and-verify/verify/author-a-verifier/) and a running server from [Set up Wyrd](/wyrd/get-started/setup/). Install the SDK with its telemetry and gateway extras, and the OpenAI client:

```bash
uv add "wyrd-ai[otel,gateway]==0.3.0" openai
```

## 1. Connect at startup

Once, when your app starts:

```python title="desk.py"
from openai import DefaultHttpxClient, OpenAI
from wyrd import WyrdClient, WyrdState

client = WyrdClient()  # finds the server and credential wyrd init saved
state = WyrdState.declare("service/support-desk.yaml", client)
state.start_bifrost()    # the writer for rows and verdict inputs
state.start_telemetry()  # exports spans started inside a Run

# Your model calls go through Wyrd's gateway. http_auth signs each call and
# ties it to the Run it is made in.
gateway = OpenAI(
    base_url=f"{client.server_url}/v1",
    api_key="wyrd",  # placeholder; http_auth replaces it
    http_client=DefaultHttpxClient(auth=client.http_auth),
)
prompt = state.prompt("prompt").prompt  # the Service's declared Prompt
```

`start_bifrost` is the first server call, so a wrong URL or credential fails here, at startup.

## 2. Answer inside a Run

Open a Run per request, and a view of the agent for the work the agent does:

```python title="desk.py"
def answer(question: str):
    with state.run() as run, run.for_card("agent") as agent:
        # Fill the Prompt's {{question}}; a missing variable raises instead of sending.
        messages = prompt.render(question=question).messages
        # Recorded by the gateway under this Run and the agent.
        reply = gateway.chat.completions.create(model="openai/gpt-4o", messages=messages)
        text = reply.choices[0].message.content

        # A row in the Service's tickets table, tagged with this Run.
        run.observe.record("vala.datasets.tickets", {"question": question, "answer": text})
        return run, agent, text
```

`openai/gpt-4o` is `<deployment>/<model>`: the [LLM gateway](/wyrd/connect/set-up-the-llm-gateway/) deployment, then the model it sends upstream.

## 3. Verify the answer

Call each Verifier on the view it is bound to. `no-refund-promise` is bound to the Service, so it runs on `run`; `ticket-complete` is bound to the agent, so it runs on `agent`:

```python title="desk.py"
run, agent, text = answer("Can I get my money back?")

checked = run.observe.verify("no-refund-promise", answer=text)
ticket = agent.observe.verify("ticket-complete", ticket={"answer": text, "order_id": "A-1001"})
print(checked.verdict, ticket.verdict)
```

```text
passed passed
```

`verify` waits for the verdict. For a slow check, such as a model judge, `submit` queues it and returns an execution instead:

```python title="desk.py"
from wyrd import verify

execution = agent.observe.submit("follows-policy", letter=verify.File("letter.md"))
print(execution.id)
```

Read it back later, from any process, by that ID:

```python
status = verify.Execution.connect(execution_id, client).status()
print(status["status"])  # pending, running, or completed
```

## 4. Shut down cleanly

Rows and spans are sent in batches. Send what is still queued when the process stops:

```python
state.shutdown()
```

A process killed without it can lose its last rows and spans.

## 5. Read the Run back

Every row the Run produced carries its `run_id`, so one query joins the ticket, the gateway call, and each verdict:

```sql title="run.sql"
SELECT t.question, t.answer, g.call_id, r.verdict
FROM vala.datasets.tickets t
JOIN vala.gateway.calls g ON g.run_id = t.run_id
JOIN vala.verification.results r ON r.run_id = t.run_id
WHERE t.run_id = $1
```

```python
from wyrd.bifrost import Bifrost

rows = Bifrost().sql(open("run.sql").read(), [run.run_id]).to_arrow().to_pylist()
print(rows)
```

Rows become queryable a few seconds after `shutdown`. An empty result right away is not proof they are missing; query again.

**In production:**

Pull the exact Service version at deploy time with `wyrd pull`, load it with `WyrdState.from_path`, and give the app a key bound to that Service. [ASGI apps](/wyrd/connect/integrate-asgi/) shows it.

## If it fails

| You see | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `WYRD_SDK_400_BIFROST_NOT_STARTED` | Call `state.start_bifrost()` at startup, before any `observe` call |
| `WYRD_SDK_404_UNKNOWN_VERIFIER` | Call the Verifier on the view it is bound to: `run` for the Service, `agent` for the agent |
| `WYRD_VALA_404_BIFROST_TABLE_NOT_FOUND` | Declare the table under the Service's `spec.tables` |
| `WYRD_VALA_403_BIFROST_CARD_SCOPE` at `shutdown` | Use a key issued for this Service version |

## Next

[Runs and evidence](/wyrd/understand/runs-observations-and-evidence/) explains what a Run records and how long it is kept.

# Write a Verifier

Page: /wyrd/build-and-verify/verify/author-a-verifier/

> Write a Verifier, bind it to your Service, call it from your code, and read its verdict, then add a Python check and a model judge.

Build the Verifiers for a support desk: one assertion, one Python check, and one model judge. Each step adds a check, binds it, and shows the verdict your code gets back.

You need a running server from [Set up Wyrd](/wyrd/get-started/setup/). The files live in a `service/` directory next to your program.

## 1. Write an assertion

A Verifier names the evidence it takes and what must be true of it. This one fails any answer that promises a guaranteed refund:

```yaml title="service/no-refund-promise.yaml"
# The Service-wide check: whatever component answers, the desk never promises
# a guaranteed refund. One assertion, no model.
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Verifier
metadata:
  name: no-refund-promise
  version: 1.0.0
spec:
  description: A support answer never promises a guaranteed refund.
  inputs:
    answer: {type: json}  # a named slot your code fills; json takes any JSON value
  requirements:  # each requirement gets its own verdict
    - id: no-refund-promise
      statement: The answer never promises a guaranteed refund  # shown in results
      # compare the value at path with expected; no model runs
      check: {kind: assert, path: inputs.answer, operator: not_contains, expected: guaranteed refund}

```

An assertion runs no model, so its verdict is deterministic and returns in milliseconds. Every field is listed in the [Verifier Card reference](/wyrd/reference/verifier-card/).

## 2. Bind it and check it

A Verifier runs only on what it is bound to. Add it under `verified_by` in your Service:

```yaml title="service/support-desk.yaml"
spec:
  verified_by:
    - verifier: ./no-refund-promise.yaml  # runs on the Service itself
```

Check every file without declaring anything:

```bash
wyrd declare --check service/support-desk.yaml
```

A misspelled field or a reference to a slot that does not exist fails here, naming the field.

## 3. Call it and read the verdict

Open a Run for each request your app handles, and verify the answer inside it:

```python title="app.py"
from wyrd import WyrdState

state = WyrdState.declare("service/support-desk.yaml")  # declares only what changed

with state.run() as run:  # one Run per request; everything inside is tied to it
    answer = support_agent("Can I get my money back?")  # your agent's own code
    # answer= fills the Verifier's answer slot; verify waits for the verdict
    result = run.observe.verify("no-refund-promise", answer=answer)

print(result.verdict)
for requirement in result.requirements:  # one outcome and reason per requirement
    print(requirement["id"], requirement["outcome"], requirement["reason"])
```

```bash
uv run python app.py
```

```text
passed
no-refund-promise passed ...
```

A `failed` verdict is an ordinary return, not an exception: the check ran and the answer broke the rule.

## 4. Add a Python check

When one operator cannot express the rule, write it in Python. This Verifier names every field a ticket is missing:

```yaml title="service/ticket-complete.yaml"
# A code check: sandboxed Python reads the ticket and names every field the
# help desk needs that is missing. No model.
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Verifier
metadata:
  name: ticket-complete
  version: 1.0.0
spec:
  description: A support ticket carries the fields the help desk needs.
  inputs:
    ticket: {type: json}
  requirements:
    - id: ticket-complete
      statement: The ticket has an answer and an order id
      check:
        kind: code
        entrypoint: check  # the function Wyrd calls
        inputs: {ticket: inputs.ticket}  # its arguments, read from the evidence
        source:
          inline: |
            def check(ticket):
                missing = [field for field in ("answer", "order_id") if not ticket.get(field)]
                return {  # the requirement's verdict
                    "outcome": "failed" if missing else "passed",
                    "reason": "missing " + ", ".join(missing) if missing else "all fields present",
                    "citations": [{"slot": "ticket", "locator": {"json_pointer": ""}}],
                }

```

The function must return the requirement's [verdict](/wyrd/reference/verifier-card/#verdicts-and-citations), with exactly these fields:

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `outcome` | `passed`, `failed`, or `inconclusive` |
| `reason` | One sentence shown in the result |
| `citations` | Where in the evidence the decision rests, as `{slot, locator}` |

Any other shape, or an exception, makes the requirement `inconclusive`, and so does a `passed` outcome without a citation. The same function used as a step instead of a check may return any JSON. The code runs in Wyrd's sandbox with no files, network, or environment.

Tickets come from the agent, so bind this Verifier to the agent component rather than the whole Service:

```yaml title="service/support-desk.yaml"
spec:
  components:
    - alias: agent
      ref: ./support-agent.yaml
      verified_by:
        - verifier: ./ticket-complete.yaml
```

Verify on the Run's view of that component, inside the same `with` block:

```python
result = run.for_card("agent").observe.verify("ticket-complete", ticket={"answer": answer, "order_id": "A-1001"})
print(result.verdict)  # passed
```

## 5. Add a model judge

Some rules need judgment. `follows-policy` asks a model whether a refund decision letter follows the refund policy, which lives in the judge Agent's prompt:

**follows-policy.yaml**

```yaml title="service/follows-policy.yaml"
# The support agent writes a refund decision letter; this Verifier checks the
# letter against the refund policy. The policy is fixed in policy-judge's
# prompt, so the letter is the only evidence the app sends, and a new policy
# means a new judge and Verifier version. The judge calls a model, so the app
# runs this one in the background.
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Verifier
metadata:
  name: follows-policy
  version: 1.0.0
spec:
  description: A refund decision letter follows the refund policy.
  inputs:
    letter: {type: media, formats: [markdown], max_bytes: 1048576}
  steps:
    # Turn the uploaded file into text the judge can read and cite by line.
    - id: read-letter
      action: {kind: extract, from: inputs.letter}
  requirements:
    - id: follows-policy
      statement: The letter's refund decision follows the refund policy
      check:
        kind: agent
        agent: ./policy-judge.yaml
        inputs:
          claim: requirement.statement
          letter: steps.read-letter.output

```

**policy-judge.yaml**

```yaml title="service/policy-judge.yaml"
# A tool-less judge. The refund policy lives in its prompt, so every verdict
# names the exact policy it applied. It returns a Verdict that cites the
# lines of the letter it relied on.
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Agent
metadata:
  name: policy-judge
  version: 1.0.0
spec:
  execution_route: {kind: wyrd_gateway, deployment: openai}
  run_config: {max_iterations: 1}
  prompt:
    provider: openai
    model: gpt-6-luna
    system: |
      You check refund decision letters against this refund policy:
      1. Refunds of up to 100 dollars are approved within 30 days of purchase.
      2. Larger refunds need a manager's approval.
      Cite the lines of the letter your judgment rests on.
    messages:
      - role: user
        content: "Claim: {{claim}}. Letter: {{letter}}"
    response_format: verdict

```

The judge calls its model through your server's [LLM gateway](/wyrd/connect/set-up-the-llm-gateway/), on the deployment named in `execution_route`. Its `response_format` must be the same verdict schema, or declaring the Verifier fails. Bind `follows-policy` beside `ticket-complete` on the agent.

A model call takes seconds, so submit the letter and collect the verdict later instead of waiting in the request:

```python
from wyrd import verify

# inside the same with block
execution = run.for_card("agent").observe.submit("follows-policy", letter=verify.File("letter.md"))
result = execution.wait(timeout=60)  # or later, from any process: verify.Execution.connect(id)
print(result.verdict)  # passed
```

## If it fails

| You see | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `WYRD_REGISTRY_400_INVALID_CARD_SPEC` naming an unknown field | Fix the spelling against the [Verifier Card reference](/wyrd/reference/verifier-card/) |
| `WYRD_SPEC_400_VALIDATION` with rule `unknown_reference` | Match the slot or step `id` the reference names |
| `WYRD_SDK_404_UNKNOWN_VERIFIER` | Verify on the view the Verifier is bound to: `run` for the Service, `run.for_card("agent")` for the agent |
| `WYRD_GATEWAY_404_MODEL_UNAVAILABLE` from the judge | Create the deployment the judge's `execution_route` names, as in [LLM gateway](/wyrd/connect/set-up-the-llm-gateway/) |

## Next

Copy a check for your own case from [Recipes](/wyrd/build-and-verify/verify/verifier-recipes/).

# Recipes

Page: /wyrd/build-and-verify/verify/verifier-recipes/

> Copyable Verifiers for common checks, each with its YAML and the Python that calls it - assertions, traces, Python checks, model judges, multi-step, grouped sessions, and drift.

Pick the check you need, bind its Verifier under `verified_by` to what it checks (a Service, one of its Agents, Models, or Data, or a standalone Agent), and call it from your code. Each recipe's Python declares `support-reply.yaml`, a Service that binds the recipe's Verifier, as in [Run your first verification](/wyrd/get-started/quickstart/).

| To check | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Fields of an answer | [Assertions](#assertions) |
| That your code took the right steps | [Trace](#trace) |
| Logic an operator cannot express | [Python check](#python-check) |
| Meaning, tone, or policy | [Model judge](#model-judge) |
| An answer against a document | [Multi-step](#multi-step) |
| A whole conversation, not one reply | [Grouped session](#grouped-session) |
| Inputs or outputs shifting over time | [Drift](#drift) |

Start with the cheapest check that catches the failure. A model judge costs a model call per requirement; an assertion costs nothing.

## Assertions

Compare fields of a JSON value with an operator.

**Declare (YAML)**

```yaml title="reply-rules.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Verifier
metadata: {name: reply-rules, version: 1.0.0}  # the name your code calls
spec:
  description: A support reply never promises a refund and stays within the refund limit.
  inputs:
    answer: {type: json}  # one named slot for the evidence; json takes any JSON value
  requirements:  # each requirement gets its own verdict
    - id: no-guarantee
      statement: The reply never promises a guaranteed refund  # shown in results
      # path selects a value from the evidence; operator compares it with expected
      check: {kind: assert, path: inputs.answer.text, operator: not_contains, expected: guaranteed refund}
    - id: within-limit
      statement: The refund offered is at most 100 dollars
      # operators that take parameters are written as {kind: ..., ...}
      check: {kind: assert, path: inputs.answer.refund, operator: {kind: in_range, min: 0, max: 100, inclusive: true}}
```

**Observe (Python)**

```python
from wyrd import WyrdState

# Declare your Service and the Verifiers it binds, then start a Run.
run = WyrdState.declare("support-reply.yaml").run()

# Pass the evidence by slot name: answer fills inputs.answer. verify waits for the verdict.
result = run.observe.verify("reply-rules", answer={"text": "Your refund is approved.", "refund": 40})
print(result.verdict)  # passed
for requirement in result.requirements:  # one verdict and reason per requirement
    print(requirement["id"], requirement["outcome"], requirement["reason"])
```

[Comparison operators](/wyrd/reference/verifier-card/#comparison-operators) lists every operator.

## Trace

Check the spans your code recorded: that a step ran, in order, with the right attributes.

**Declare (YAML)**

```yaml title="looked-up-policy.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Verifier
metadata: {name: looked-up-policy, version: 1.0.0}
spec:
  description: The reply was drafted after looking up the refunds policy.
  inputs:
    trace: {type: trace}  # a trace ID; Wyrd reads the trace's stored spans
  requirements:
    - id: looked-up-first
      statement: The first span is the policy lookup
      # spans are ordered by start time, so spans[0] is the first one
      check: {kind: trace, on: inputs.trace, span_selector: "$.spans[0].name", operator: equals, expected: lookup-policy}
    - id: read-refunds
      statement: The lookup read the refunds policy
      # attributes are the ones your code set on the span
      check: {kind: trace, on: inputs.trace, span_selector: "$.spans[0].attributes.policy_id", operator: equals, expected: refunds}
```

**Observe (Python)**

```python
from opentelemetry import trace
from wyrd import WyrdState

state = WyrdState.declare("support-reply.yaml")
state.start_telemetry()  # export OpenTelemetry spans to Wyrd
tracer = trace.get_tracer("support")

# Your code's real work, traced as it runs.
with tracer.start_as_current_span("lookup-policy", attributes={"policy_id": "refunds"}) as span:
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("draft-answer"):
        ...
state.flush()  # make sure the spans are stored before they are checked

trace_id = format(span.get_span_context().trace_id, "032x")  # 32 hex characters
result = state.run().observe.verify("looked-up-policy", trace=trace_id)
print(result.verdict)  # passed
```

## Python check

Run your own function when no operator fits. It returns a verdict with a reason and a citation.

**Declare (YAML)**

```yaml title="names-the-policy.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Verifier
metadata: {name: names-the-policy, version: 1.0.0}
spec:
  description: A support reply points the customer to the refund policy.
  inputs:
    answer: {type: json}
  requirements:
    - id: names-the-policy
      statement: The reply names the refund policy
      check:
        kind: code
        entrypoint: check  # the function to call
        inputs: {answer: inputs.answer}  # passed to it as keyword arguments
        source:
          inline: |
            def check(answer):
                named = "policy" in answer["text"].lower()
                # Return a verdict: outcome, reason, and the evidence it cites.
                return {
                    "outcome": "passed" if named else "failed",
                    "reason": "names the policy" if named else "does not name the policy",
                    # slot names an input; json_pointer points inside it
                    "citations": [{"slot": "answer", "locator": {"json_pointer": "/text"}}],
                }
```

**Observe (Python)**

```python
from wyrd import WyrdState

run = WyrdState.declare("support-reply.yaml").run()

# The function runs on the server, not in your process.
result = run.observe.verify("names-the-policy", answer={"text": "Refunds follow our policy."})
print(result.verdict)  # passed
```

The function runs sandboxed, with no files, network, or environment.

## Model judge

Ask a model whether a claim holds. A pass must cite the evidence it relied on, or it counts as `inconclusive`.

**Declare (YAML)**

```yaml title="follows-policy.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Verifier
metadata: {name: follows-policy, version: 1.0.0}
spec:
  description: A model judges whether a support reply follows the refund policy.
  inputs:
    answer: {type: json}
  requirements:
    - id: follows-policy
      statement: The reply follows the refund policy and never promises more than it allows
      check:
        kind: agent
        agent: ./policy-judge.yaml  # the judge, below
        inputs:  # fill the judge's prompt placeholders
          claim: requirement.statement  # this requirement's statement
          answer: inputs.answer.text
```

```yaml title="policy-judge.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Agent
metadata: {name: policy-judge, version: 1.0.0}
spec:
  execution_route: {kind: wyrd_gateway, deployment: openai}  # a deployment in your LLM gateway
  run_config: {max_iterations: 1}  # one model call, no tools
  prompt:
    provider: openai
    model: gpt-4o
    messages:
      - role: user
        content: |
          Refunds of up to 100 dollars are approved within 30 days; larger refunds need a manager.
          Claim: {{claim}}  # filled from the check's inputs
          Reply: {{answer}}
          Decide whether the claim holds for the reply, and cite the reply.
    # The judge answers with a Verdict: an outcome, a reason, and citations.
    response_format: verdict
```

**Observe (Python)**

```python
from wyrd import WyrdState

run = WyrdState.declare("support-reply.yaml").run()

result = run.observe.verify("follows-policy", answer={"text": "Refunds up to 100 dollars follow our policy."})
judged = result.requirements[0]
print(judged["outcome"], judged["reason"])  # the judge's verdict and its explanation
print(judged.get("citations"))  # where in the reply the judge looked
```

The judge's model calls go through the LLM gateway with your provider key. [Verdicts and citations](/wyrd/reference/verifier-card/#verdicts-and-citations) explains the locators a citation can use.

### Return scores and labels with the verdict

Declare a schema under `data` and the judge returns that object beside its verdict. The server checks it against the schema; output that does not match is `inconclusive` and keeps no data.

```yaml title="policy-judge.yaml (excerpt)"
    response_format:
      kind: verdict
      data:
        type: object
        properties:
          score: {type: number, minimum: 0, maximum: 1}
          category: {type: string}
        required: [score, category]
        additionalProperties: false
```

A `code` check declares the same `response_format` beside `entrypoint`, and its function returns `data` with its verdict. Each requirement carries its own `data`, which stays absent when its check declares none. Read it as JSON, or ask for your own type:

**Python**

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel

class JudgeData(BaseModel):
    score: float
    category: str

result = run.observe.verify_typed("follows-policy", JudgeData, answer={"text": "Refunds up to 100 dollars follow our policy."})
data = result.requirements[0].get("data")  # a JudgeData, or None when the check returned none
```

**Rust**

```rust
use serde::Deserialize;
use serde_json::json;
use wyrd_ai::verify::{Input, Inputs};

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct JudgeData {
    score: f64,
    category: String,
}

let answer = json!({ "text": "Refunds up to 100 dollars follow our policy." });
let result = run
    .observe()
    .verify_typed::<JudgeData>("follows-policy", Inputs::named([("answer", Input::from(answer))]))
    .await?;
let data = result.outcome.requirements[0].data.as_ref(); // a JudgeData, or None when the check returned none
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
import { z } from "zod";

const JudgeData = z.object({ score: z.number(), category: z.string() });

const answer = { text: "Refunds up to 100 dollars follow our policy." };
const result = await run.observe.verifyTyped("follows-policy", { answer }, JudgeData);
const data = result.outcome.requirements[0]?.data; // a JudgeData, or undefined when the check returned none
```

Data that does not fit your type raises `WYRD_SDK_422_VERIFICATION_DATA_INVALID` naming the requirement; the stored result is unchanged and nothing runs again. Its `path` is always `""`, the root of that requirement's data, because a deeper path could name a key the check returned.

## Multi-step

Prepare evidence before checking it. Here a step reads the policy PDF, a second step compares the refund with the limit it states, and a requirement checks the result.

**Declare (YAML)**

```yaml title="within-policy.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Verifier
metadata: {name: within-policy, version: 1.0.0}
spec:
  description: The refund offered is within the limit the policy PDF states.
  inputs:
    answer: {type: json}
    policy: {type: media, formats: [pdf]}  # a file, uploaded by your code
  steps:  # run before the requirements; later steps read earlier outputs
    - id: policy-text
      action: {kind: extract, from: inputs.policy}  # PDF to text, page by page
    - id: compare
      action:
        kind: code
        entrypoint: compare
        # steps.<id>.output reads a step's result; this step waits for policy-text
        inputs: {pages: steps.policy-text.output.pages, answer: inputs.answer}
        source:
          inline: |
            def compare(pages, answer):
                text = " ".join(page["text"] for page in pages)
                # "Refunds of up to 100 dollars are approved ..."
                limit = int(text.split("up to ")[1].split(" ")[0])
                return {"within_limit": answer["refund"] <= limit}
  requirements:
    - id: within-limit
      statement: The refund offered is within the policy limit
      check: {kind: assert, path: steps.compare.output.within_limit, operator: equals, expected: true}  # reads the step's output
```

**Observe (Python)**

```python
from wyrd import WyrdState, verify

run = WyrdState.declare("support-reply.yaml").run()

# One keyword per input slot.
result = run.observe.verify(
    "within-policy",
    answer={"text": "Your refund of 40 dollars is approved.", "refund": 40},
    policy=verify.File("refund-policy.pdf"),  # your policy document, with "up to N dollars"
)
print(result.verdict)  # passed
for step in result.steps:  # each step's status, for debugging
    print(step["id"], step["status"])
```

Steps can also be `agent` actions, which read files with built-in tools. [Actions](/wyrd/reference/verifier-card/#actions) lists each kind.

## Grouped session

Judge a whole conversation after it ends. Each reply is verified on its own; a session Verifier reads every reply's evidence and outcome once the group goes quiet.

**Declare (YAML)**

```yaml title="whole-conversation.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Verifier
metadata: {name: whole-conversation, version: 1.0.0}
spec:
  description: Every reply of a conversation passed reply-rules.
  inputs:
    # Every reply-rules answer in the group, in order.
    replies: verifiers.reply-rules.inputs.answer
    # Every no-guarantee outcome in the group: passed, failed, or inconclusive.
    outcomes: verifiers.reply-rules.requirements.no-guarantee.outcome
  # List order: recorded_at (the default) is the order Wyrd received each reply;
  # inputs.replies.<field> orders by a field of each reply instead.
  order_by: recorded_at
  requirements:
    - id: every-reply-passed
      statement: No reply in the conversation promised a guaranteed refund
      # each checks every item; one failed reply fails the conversation
      check: {kind: assert, each: "inputs.outcomes[*]", operator: equals, expected: passed}
```

Bind it beside `reply-rules` with a `group_end` Trigger:

```yaml
verified_by:
  - verifier: ./reply-rules.yaml
  - verifier: ./whole-conversation.yaml
    runs_on: {kind: group_end, after: 10m}  # judge 10 minutes after the last reply
```

**Observe (Python)**

```python
from wyrd import WyrdState

run = WyrdState.declare("support-reply.yaml").run()
conversation = "conv-1234"  # one ID per conversation
replies = [
    {"text": "Let me check your order.", "refund": 0},
    {"text": "Your refund of 40 dollars is approved.", "refund": 40},
]

for reply in replies:
    # Each reply is judged now; group_id also adds it to the conversation.
    run.observe.verify("reply-rules", answer=reply, group_id=conversation)
# whole-conversation runs on its own, 10 minutes after the last reply.
```

New replies in the group push the session check back. Its verdict is stored in `vala.verification.results` with the `group_id`.

## Drift

Compare recent values with a baseline on a schedule. Your code records samples; the schedule judges the window.

**Declare (YAML)**

```yaml title="latency-drift.yaml"
apiVersion: wyrd/v1
kind: Verifier
metadata: {name: latency-drift, version: 1.0.0}
spec:
  description: Request latency stays distributed like the healthy baseline.
  inputs:
    latency: {type: samples, features: [latency]}  # values your code records over time
  requirements:
    - id: latency-stable
      statement: Request latency is distributed like the healthy baseline
      check:
        kind: drift
        on: inputs.latency
        method: Psi  # Population Stability Index: how far a distribution moved
        signal:
          kind: Distribution
          baseline_ref: {kind: Data, name: latency-baseline, version: 1.0.0}  # what healthy looks like
          features: [latency]
        condition: {kind: Statistical}
        profile:
          kind: Psi
          binning_strategy: {kind: EqualWidth, n_bins: 10}  # compare across 10 equal-width buckets
          threshold: {kind: Fixed, value: 0.25}  # fail when PSI is above 0.25
```

Bind it with a schedule:

```yaml
verified_by:
  - verifier: ./latency-drift.yaml
    runs_on: {kind: schedule, cron: "0 0 * * *"}  # judge the day's samples at midnight
```

**Observe (Python)**

```python
import pandas as pd
from wyrd import WyrdState
from wyrd.cards import Cards
from wyrd.data import DataCard, PandasInterface

# Declare the baseline once: latencies from healthy traffic, in milliseconds.
healthy = pd.DataFrame({"latency": [float(ms) for ms in range(100)]})
Cards().data.declare(DataCard(PandasInterface(data=healthy), name="latency-baseline", version="1.0.0"))

run = WyrdState.declare("support-reply.yaml").run()
run.observe.submit("latency-drift", latency={"latency": 12.5})  # one sample per request
```

A drift Verifier refuses `verify`; only the schedule judges it.

## Next

[How verification works](/wyrd/understand/how-verification-works/) explains steps, verdicts, and where each check runs.

# LLM gateway

Page: /wyrd/connect/set-up-the-llm-gateway/

> Store a provider key on your Wyrd server, create a deployment for it, and call the model through Wyrd with your Wyrd credential.

Call OpenAI through your Wyrd server. Your code signs in to Wyrd, Wyrd adds the provider key and records the call, and the key never leaves the server.

You need a running server from [Set up Wyrd](/wyrd/get-started/setup/) and an OpenAI key in `OPENAI_API_KEY`.

**Already offered at setup:**

If you accepted the gateway offer during `wyrd init`, the `openai` deployment exists. Skip to step 3.

## 1. Store the key

```bash
wyrd gateway credential put --file - <<JSON
{"name": "openai-key", "provider": "openai", "source": {"managed_secret": {"secret": "$OPENAI_API_KEY"}}}
JSON
```

The key goes to the server over stdin, so it never lands in a file or your shell history. The server encrypts it, and every read of it is redacted.

## 2. Create the deployment

A deployment names a provider and the key to call it with. Your code addresses models through it. The name is yours, so one provider can have several deployments, such as one per team or caller, each with its own key:

```bash
wyrd gateway deployment put --file - <<'JSON'
{"name": "openai", "adapter": "openai", "auth": {"bearer": {"credential": "openai-key"}}}
JSON
```

## 3. Turn on recording

A new tenant records no calls. Record each call's caller, model, outcome, and token usage, without the prompt or reply:

```bash
wyrd gateway capture-policy put --file - <<'JSON'
{"mode": "metadata", "payload_fields": []}
JSON
```

Calls made before this step are never recorded.

## 4. Make a request

```bash
uv add "wyrd-ai[gateway]==0.3.0" openai
```

```python title="call.py"
from openai import DefaultHttpxClient, OpenAI
from wyrd import WyrdClient

wyrd = WyrdClient()  # finds the server and credential wyrd init saved
client = OpenAI(
    base_url=f"{wyrd.server_url}/v1",
    api_key="wyrd",  # placeholder; http_auth replaces it with your Wyrd token
    http_client=DefaultHttpxClient(auth=wyrd.http_auth),
)

reply = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="openai/gpt-4o",  # <deployment>/<model>
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say hi."}],
)
print(reply.choices[0].message.content)
```

```bash
uv run python call.py
```

It prints the model's reply. OpenAI received `gpt-4o` with your stored key and never saw your Wyrd token.

## 5. Check the call was recorded

```python title="calls.py"
from wyrd.bifrost import Bifrost

rows = Bifrost().sql(
    "SELECT requested_model, outcome FROM vala.gateway.calls ORDER BY started_at DESC LIMIT 1"
).to_arrow().to_pylist()
print(rows)
```

```bash
uv run python calls.py
```

```text
[{'requested_model': {'deployment': 'openai', 'model': 'gpt-4o'}, 'outcome': 'succeeded'}]
```

Rows appear a few seconds after the call. If the result is empty, query again.

## Add another provider

Repeat steps 1 and 2 with that provider's key and authentication:

| Provider | `provider` and `adapter` | `auth` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OpenAI | `openai` | `{"bearer": {"credential": "openai-key"}}` |
| Anthropic | `anthropic` | `{"api_key_header": {"header": "x-api-key", "credential": "anthropic-key"}}` |
| Gemini | `gemini` | `{"api_key_header": {"header": "x-goog-api-key", "credential": "gemini-key"}}` |

## If it fails

| You see | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `WYRD_GATEWAY_404_MODEL_UNAVAILABLE` | Check the deployment name with `wyrd gateway deployment list` |
| `WYRD_GATEWAY_502_UPSTREAM_UNAVAILABLE` | Check the key with `wyrd gateway credential get openai-key`, and that the provider is reachable |
| `WYRD_CLIENT_401_NO_CREDENTIALS` | Run `wyrd init` in this directory, or set `WYRD_API_KEY` |
| The query in step 5 stays empty | Run `wyrd gateway capture-policy get`; if it says `disabled`, repeat step 3 |

## Next

Judge answers with a model in [Write a Verifier](/wyrd/build-and-verify/verify/author-a-verifier/#5-add-a-model-judge).

# ASGI apps

Page: /wyrd/connect/integrate-asgi/

> Add WyrdMiddleware to a FastAPI, Starlette, Django, or Litestar app to start Wyrd with the app, verify inside one Run per request, and drain queued evidence at shutdown.

Add `WyrdMiddleware` to any ASGI app, such as FastAPI, Starlette, Django, or Litestar. It starts Wyrd when your app starts, wraps each request in its own Run, and sends queued evidence when your app stops.

## What you capture

- One Run per HTTP request or WebSocket connection. Every verdict and row the request produces shares that Run's `run_id`.
- Spans your OpenTelemetry instrumentation records inside the Run, tagged with its `wyrd.run_id` and `wyrd.card_uid`.

## Before you start

- The server from [Set up Wyrd](/wyrd/get-started/setup/), running.
- The `support-reply` Service from [Run your first verification](/wyrd/get-started/quickstart/), declared.

## Install

```bash
uv add "wyrd-ai[otel]==0.3.0" uvicorn
```

Add your framework too, such as `uv add fastapi`. Then pull the Service into the app's directory, at build or deploy time rather than when the app starts:

```bash
uv run wyrd pull --kind Service --name support-reply --version 1.0.0 --output-dir .wyrd-bundle
```

## Usage

Each app loads the pulled Service, adds the middleware, and reads the request's Run in its handler:

**FastAPI**

```python title="app.py"
"""A FastAPI app that verifies each support answer it receives under its own Run.

It serves the Quickstart's ``support-reply`` Service, pulled once at deploy time:

    wyrd pull --kind Service --name support-reply --version 1.0.0 \
      --output-dir .wyrd-bundle
    uv run uvicorn app:app
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio

from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from pydantic import BaseModel
from wyrd.integrations.asgi import RUN_SCOPE_KEY, WyrdMiddleware
from wyrd.state import WyrdState

# Load the pulled Service; this reads local files only.
state = WyrdState.from_path(".wyrd-bundle")

app = FastAPI()
# Start the state with the app, drain it at shutdown, and open one Run per request.
app.add_middleware(WyrdMiddleware, state=state)

class Reply(BaseModel):
    answer: str

@app.post("/replies")
async def check_reply(reply: Reply, request: Request) -> dict[str, str]:
    # This request's Run, opened by the middleware.
    run = request.scope[RUN_SCOPE_KEY]
    # Verification waits for the verdict, so it runs off the event loop.
    result = await asyncio.to_thread(run.observe.verify, "no-refund-promise", answer=reply.answer)
    return {"run_id": run.run_id, "verdict": result.verdict}

```

```bash
uv run uvicorn app:app
```

**Starlette**

```python title="app.py"
import asyncio

from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.middleware import Middleware
from starlette.responses import JSONResponse
from starlette.routing import Route
from wyrd.integrations.asgi import RUN_SCOPE_KEY, WyrdMiddleware
from wyrd.state import WyrdState

state = WyrdState.from_path(".wyrd-bundle")  # reads local files only

async def check_reply(request):
    run = request.scope[RUN_SCOPE_KEY]  # this request's Run, opened by the middleware
    answer = (await request.json())["answer"]
    # verify waits for the verdict, so it runs off the event loop
    result = await asyncio.to_thread(run.observe.verify, "no-refund-promise", answer=answer)
    return JSONResponse({"run_id": run.run_id, "verdict": result.verdict})

app = Starlette(
    routes=[Route("/replies", check_reply, methods=["POST"])],
    middleware=[Middleware(WyrdMiddleware, state=state)],
)
```

```bash
uv run uvicorn app:app
```

**Django**

Wrap the ASGI application in `asgi.py`:

```python title="mysite/asgi.py"
import os

from django.core.asgi import get_asgi_application
from wyrd.integrations.asgi import WyrdMiddleware
from wyrd.state import WyrdState

os.environ.setdefault("DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE", "mysite.settings")
application = WyrdMiddleware(get_asgi_application(), state=WyrdState.from_path(".wyrd-bundle"))
```

Then read the Run in a view:

```python title="replies/views.py"
import json

from django.http import JsonResponse
from django.views.decorators.csrf import csrf_exempt
from wyrd.integrations.asgi import RUN_SCOPE_KEY

@csrf_exempt  # so the curl below can post without a CSRF token
def check_reply(request):
    run = request.scope[RUN_SCOPE_KEY]  # this request's Run, opened by the middleware
    answer = json.loads(request.body)["answer"]
    result = run.observe.verify("no-refund-promise", answer=answer)
    return JsonResponse({"run_id": run.run_id, "verdict": result.verdict})
```

Add `path("replies", check_reply)` to `urlpatterns` in `urls.py`, then serve it:

```bash
uv run uvicorn mysite.asgi:application
```

**Litestar**

```python title="app.py"
import asyncio

from litestar import Litestar, Request, post
from wyrd.integrations.asgi import RUN_SCOPE_KEY, WyrdMiddleware
from wyrd.state import WyrdState

state = WyrdState.from_path(".wyrd-bundle")  # reads local files only

@post("/replies")
async def check_reply(request: Request, data: dict[str, str]) -> dict[str, str]:
    run = request.scope[RUN_SCOPE_KEY]  # this request's Run, opened by the middleware
    # verify waits for the verdict, so it runs off the event loop
    result = await asyncio.to_thread(run.observe.verify, "no-refund-promise", answer=data["answer"])
    return {"run_id": run.run_id, "verdict": result.verdict}

app = WyrdMiddleware(Litestar([check_reply]), state=state)  # wraps any ASGI app
```

```bash
uv run uvicorn app:app
```

What the middleware does:

| When | It |
| --- | --- |
| The app starts | Starts Wyrd's writer and telemetry, before your app's own startup. If either fails, the app does not start. |
| A request arrives | Opens a Run of the Service, puts it at `request.scope["wyrd.run"]`, and runs your handler inside it. |
| The app stops | Waits for your app's own shutdown, then sends every queued row and span. |

The middleware verifies nothing by itself. Your handler decides what to verify and records it on the request's Run.

## Verify it worked

In a second terminal, send an answer that breaks the requirement:

```bash
curl -s localhost:8000/replies -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"answer": "You have a guaranteed refund."}'
```

The reply names the request's Run and a `failed` verdict. A second request returns a different `run_id`.

## If it fails

| You see | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Startup fails with `WYRD_SDK_409_TELEMETRY_PROVIDER_EXISTS` | Your app installs its own tracer provider: pass `telemetry=False` and add `wyrd.otel.span_exporter(client)` to that provider |
| Startup fails with an `ImportError` naming `otel` | Install `wyrd-ai[otel]`, or pass `telemetry=False` |
| `WYRD_SDK_400_BIFROST_NOT_STARTED` when the app records | The server runs without lifespan: leave Uvicorn's `--lifespan` at `auto` or set it to `on` |
| `WYRD_SDK_404_UNKNOWN_ALIAS` on every request | `alias` returned a name the bundle does not have |

## Advanced

### Choose the component per request

By default each Run observes the Service. To observe one of its components instead, pass `alias`, a function from the request's ASGI scope to a component alias, or `None` for the Service:

```python
def by_path(scope):
    return "agent" if scope["path"].startswith("/agent/") else None

app.add_middleware(WyrdMiddleware, state=state, alias=by_path)
```

An alias the bundle lacks fails the request before your handler runs.

### WebSockets

A WebSocket connection is one Run for its whole life, so every message on it shares one `run_id`. To judge each turn of a conversation separately and the conversation as a whole, pass a `group_id` to `verify`, as in the [grouped recipe](/wyrd/build-and-verify/verify/verifier-recipes/#grouped-session).

### Your own OpenTelemetry instrumentation

Add `WyrdMiddleware` after OpenTelemetry's ASGI or framework instrumentation, so Wyrd's middleware is outermost and the instrumentation's spans start inside the Run. The middleware creates no spans of its own. If your app owns its tracer provider, pass `telemetry=False`: the app installs, exports, and flushes that provider, and calls `wyrd.otel.install_run_correlation(provider)` once to tag spans with the Run.

### Gunicorn

Run Gunicorn with Uvicorn workers:

```bash
uv add gunicorn
uv run gunicorn app:app --workers 2 --worker-class uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker
```

Each worker starts and drains its own writer. Lifespan must stay enabled; without it nothing starts and nothing drains.

A graceful stop (`SIGTERM`) drains every worker. A worker killed with `SIGKILL`, one that exceeds `--graceful-timeout`, or a failed drain can lose queued rows.

## Reference

`WyrdMiddleware(app, *, state, telemetry=True, alias=None)`, from `wyrd.integrations.asgi`:

| Argument | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `app` | The ASGI app to wrap; `add_middleware` passes it. |
| `state` | A loaded `WyrdState`. The middleware never declares or registers anything. |
| `telemetry` | Whether startup calls `state.start_telemetry()`. Default `True`. |
| `alias` | Function from the ASGI scope to the component alias each Run observes. Default: the Service. |

`RUN_SCOPE_KEY` is `"wyrd.run"`, the scope key that holds the request's Run. Other ASGI connection types pass through unchanged.

## Next

[Runs and evidence](/wyrd/understand/runs-observations-and-evidence/) explains what a Run records and how long it is kept.

# Verification runtime

Page: /wyrd/operate/configure-verification-runtime/

> Choose which processes run Verifiers, size the worker pool, and diagnose startup refusals.

Decide which processes run Verifiers and how much Python each runs at once. Every value is in [Verification runtime limits](/wyrd/reference/verification-runtime-limits/).

## Choose which processes run Verifiers

Every API-serving process runs Verifiers by default. To keep one out, set `WYRD_VERIFICATION_ENABLED=0`, or `enabled = false` under `[verification]` in the [server TOML file](/wyrd/reference/verification-runtime-limits/#server-toml-file). Route verification traffic to the processes that keep it on.

## Size the worker pool

The server starts its own Python workers; there is nothing to install. Each process has its own pool, and a process that runs Verifiers starts its first `WYRD_VERIFICATION_MONTY_MIN_WORKERS` workers before it reports ready.

- To run more Python at once, raise `WYRD_VERIFICATION_MONTY_POOL_MEMORY_MIB` and `WYRD_VERIFICATION_MONTY_MAX_WORKERS` together.
- To give each operation more memory, raise `WYRD_VERIFICATION_MONTY_MEMORY_MIB` with `WYRD_VERIFICATION_MONTY_PROCESS_MEMORY_MIB`, which must exceed it by at least 4 MiB.
- Leave memory beyond the pool for the server, extraction, and model responses, and temporary-directory space for `WYRD_VERIFICATION_MAX_WORKSPACES` workspaces of up to `WYRD_VERIFICATION_SCRATCH_MAX_MIB` each.

Settings are read at startup; restart to apply a change.

## If it fails

| You see | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `hosted Verifier blocks could not start` | Fix the cause the rest of the message names, then restart |
| `environment variable WYRD_VERIFICATION_... could not be parsed` | Set a positive integer |
| Two variable names in a startup error | Fix the pair; see [startup rules](/wyrd/reference/verification-runtime-limits/#startup-rules) |
| `WYRD_SERVER_503_SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE` from `verify` | The process has verification off or no free worker; retry or route to another process |

## Next

[Verification runtime limits](/wyrd/reference/verification-runtime-limits/) lists every setting, its default, and what happens when a limit is reached.

# Architecture

Page: /wyrd/understand/architecture/

> What a team deployment of Wyrd runs, what it connects to, and why each part is separate.
